title: Kemi Badenoch is creating a new—and very odd—type of Tory party
gist: Rusbridger argues Kemi Badenoch's Conservative party is applying its rehabilitation and tolerance rules in reverse: a former neo-Nazi with two jail terms for antisemitism was defended as a candidate and then given an anti-extremism advisory role, while Grant Shapps and Gavin Barwell were purged for dissenting on net zero — a positioning that abandons the roughly 60 per cent of voters (and 48 per cent of Tories) who back the 2050 target and leaves the 'disillusioned centre' politically homeless.

insights.claim: Badenoch publicly defended Joshua Bonehill-Paine — who served two jail sentences for antisemitism, harassed a Jewish MP and founded the neo-Nazi National British Resistance — as a Conservative council candidate in Somerset, despite saying she is normally sceptical about rehabilitation.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A vetting failure the leader chose to own rather than disavow — an indicator of weak candidate-selection controls ahead of a general election.
insights.quote: Piling on them and trying to get them cancelled may be sport for other parties, but this is a different Conservative party,
insights.locator: Joshua Bonehill-Paine was a nasty piece of work

insights.claim: Bonehill-Paine stood down as candidate but was then announced into a new role advising Badenoch on combating extremism — an outcome the harassed former MP Luciana Berger described as an insult.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The reputational damage was doubled rather than contained — evidence of poor crisis management at the top of the party.
insights.locator: It was an odd hill for Badenoch to die on

insights.claim: Badenoch refused Louise Haigh the same second chance she granted Bonehill-Paine, attacking Starmer's 2024 appointment with the line that the country needs conviction politicians not politicians with convictions.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Documents an inconsistency opponents will weaponise; the soundbite is now a liability rather than an asset.
insights.quote: This country needs conviction politicians, not politicians with convictions,

insights.claim: After first calling donor Frank Hester's remarks about Diane Abbott racist, Badenoch reversed within days to dismiss the row as 'pure media bubble speculation' and trivia — and the £10m donation was retained.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Shows donor concentration shaping party positioning: a single £10m cheque set the line on a racism controversy.
insights.quote: pure media bubble speculation. It is not what the country cares about. This is trivia… we need to get to a place where we stop chasing people around and looking everywhere for the racism.
insights.locator: Badenoch, then business secretary, declared the remarks to be racist

insights.claim: Badenoch has imposed a moratorium barring any candidate who will not sign up to scrapping the net zero targets Theresa May agreed in June 2019, closing off internal debate on the timescale entirely.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Hard-codes an anti-net-zero platform into candidate selection — a structural, not rhetorical, signal for UK green-transition policy risk if the Tories return to power.
insights.locator: But, even as southern Europe went up in flames

insights.claim: Roughly 60 per cent of the public and 48 per cent of self-identifying Conservatives support the UK's net zero by 2050 commitment, meaning Badenoch's ban puts her at odds with nearly half her own base.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The polling makes the anti-net-zero pivot electorally costly, weakening the case that a Tory government would actually repeal the target.
insights.locator: Most polling suggests that nearly two-thirds of us

insights.claim: Grant Shapps, who held six cabinet roles under successive prime ministers, has reportedly been banned from standing again over net zero and probably ECHR exit — showing the purge reaches the party's most senior operators.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Senior institutional talent is being removed on a single-issue test, thinning the bench for any future government.
insights.locator: You may or may not admire Grant Shapps

insights.claim: Lord Gavin Barwell, May's former Downing Street chief of staff, learned he had lost the Conservative whip in the Lords from a Daily Mail article forwarded by a friend, after mild criticism of the net zero ban.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Process breakdown as much as policy: discipline is being administered via the press, signalling an unstable internal machine.
insights.quote: The decision to take the Whip away from me suggests an intolerance of criticism,
insights.locator: The same fate has apparently befallen

insights.claim: Barwell notes that none of the six leaders he served over 30 years — Major, Hague, Duncan Smith, Howard, Cameron or May — would have removed the whip from a colleague merely for criticising strategy.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A 30-year insider benchmark establishing that this is a discontinuity in Conservative practice, not normal party discipline.
insights.locator: “The best leaders are those who welcome different voices

insights.claim: Conservative cancel culture is traced to Boris Johnson, who presumed he rather than Michael Heseltine understood the British conservative tradition — after which Ken Clarke, Philip Hammond, Oliver Letwin, Nicholas Soames and Ed Vaizey were expelled for opposing a no-deal Brexit.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Positions Badenoch's purges as the continuation of a seven-year pattern, implying the broad-church model is structurally gone rather than temporarily suspended.
insights.locator: But the Conservative party, which used to pride itself

insights.claim: Badenoch has made no move toward rapprochement with the still-cancelled Heseltine, David Gauke, Dominic Grieve, Rory Stewart or Matthew Parris — an option the author argues would be canny politics and costs nothing.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The refusal of a free win suggests the constraint is not strategy but the leader's position — a marker for leadership instability.
insights.locator: Could Badenoch not have found it in her heart

insights.claim: Pollsters agree the 'disillusioned centre' — voters cool on left-wing economics but alienated by populist social conservatism, green-transition scepticism and hardline anti-immigration rhetoric — is fertile ground that Badenoch is deliberately vacating.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: An identified unserved voter bloc; whoever occupies it captures the swing that decides the next general election.
insights.quote: voters who are not in love with traditional left-wing economic policies, but who also feel alienated by populist social conservatism, green-transition scepticism and hardline anti-immigration rhetoric.
insights.locator: It’s especially odd since pollsters seem to agree

insights.claim: A large swathe of instinctively centre-right voters now find themselves politically homeless, implying available vote share sitting outside all current party offers.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Unallocated centre-right votes are the raw material for a new entrant or a Lib Dem breakout.
insights.quote: it must be dismaying to a large swathe of instinctively centre-right voters who find themselves politically homeless

insights.claim: Badenoch's decision to denounce Reform as 'woke' is dismissed as a silly summer-headline play, since being woke is the least of Nigel Farage's current problems — indicating her differentiation strategy against Reform is misfiring.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The Tory attack line on Reform is not landing, leaving the right flank contested on Reform's terms.
insights.locator: It’s obviously sensible for Badenoch to distance herself from Reform
